title: Rep Goal System (by Steve Shaw of Massive Iron) review
summary: NH reviews Steve Shaw's rep goal system (maximize every set, keep the same weight, hit a total rep goal across sets) and finds it essentially a form of evolving rep ranges. He praises how it promotes failure and stable weights but warns that an uncapped opening set can turn into an AMRAP that wrecks muscular endurance, and that adjusting sets and goals can shrink volume to 3x5 levels.
claims: The rep goal system has three basics: maximize every set, use the same weight for all working sets, and set a total rep goal across sets, adding about 5 lb once reached
The rep goal system is essentially his evolving rep ranges under another name; volume and intensity principles exist in nature and just get different names
Not capping reps per set pushes lifters toward failure
Going to failure is very important for hypertrophy; keep reps in the tank on compounds but go to failure on everything else
You can go to failure and still waste a set: in a 20-rep set the first 15 reps mostly build lactic acid and may cause artificial failure
A 'never waste a set' mentality can push lifters who don't understand intensity windows into always grinding, even to mechanical failure
His evolving rep ranges keep a ceiling (e.g. 8-12) for stability, while the rep goal system lets the first set go as high as possible
Keep the same weight across hard sets to show you can repeat the effort; he has a fallback plan if set one proves too hard
A rep goal must stay fairly high; a one-set 20-rep version would push you to a light weight and waste most reps
Reps naturally drop across sets with the same weight (e.g. 12 down to 7), and most progression shows up in the later sets
The rep goal system suits minimalist strength work with two exercises a day; his evolving ranges are built for many exercises, so he doesn't push the first set all out
Evolving set ranges add a multiplicative variable; removing both rep and set limits leaves no structure, which is why he hasn't introduced them yet
In Shaw's example of 225 lb bench for 11, 8, 6, 5, dropping to 5 suggests the AMRAP-like first set involved grinding or degraded form that destroyed muscular endurance
Ability to return to baseline (muscular endurance) is a key hypertrophy metric
Cutting sets and lowering the rep goal to cope can shrink total volume to about what a 3x5 provides
A 5 lb jump means different things on a bench or squat versus a high-rep barbell curl
Converting a 5x5 into a 25-rep goal with evolving reps is excellent; anyone who likes static rep ranges should try making them evolve
There is no magic rep range
He adds 10 lb in his system; jump size doesn't matter as long as progression continues
Overall the rep goal system is excellent and worth trying, knowing its pitfalls
